contests.title: Proposition One: Reproductive Freedom & Privacy Act

measures.questionText: Measure creating right to abortion before fetus viability, and post-viability to protect health; right to privacy; healthcare provider liability protections.
measures.officialStatement: The measure seeks to change Idaho’s laws by introducing a right to reproductive freedom and privacy including a right to abortion up to the point of the fetus’s ability to survive outside the womb. After fetal viability, there would be no general right to abortion except in cases of “medical emergency.” The “medical emergency” exception would expand Idaho’s current life exception and allow abortions when pregnant women face complicating physical conditions that threaten their life or health, “including serious impairment to a bodily function” or “serious dysfunction of any bodily organ or part.” The proposed measure codifies a right to make reproductive decisions, including contraception, fertility treatment, and prenatal and postpartum care. This includes a “right of privacy” in making these decisions. The measure seeks to prevent the state from enforcing certain abortion laws protecting the life of the unborn child. It would also impose a requirement that any restrictions on reproductive decisions, including abortion prior to fetus viability, must be “narrowly tailored to improve or maintain the health of the person seeking reproductive health care.” The measure would also prevent the state from penalizing patients, healthcare providers, or anyone who assists in exercising the proposed right.

This advisory question asks Idahoans to designate which gun they would like to have as the official Idaho State Gun. This is a non-binding measure, and the Legislature would have to take action during a future legislative session to officially designate a gun as the Idaho State Gun.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Would create a legal right to make private reproductive health care decisions, including abortion, contraception, fertility treatment, childbirth, miscarriage care, and care before, during and after pregnancy. Abortion would be protected before fetal viability, which a physician would determine case by case based on the likelihood of sustained survival outside the uterus without extraordinary medical measures. After viability, the state could regulate abortion except for a physical medical emergency threatening the pregnant patient’s life or risking serious harm to their health, a bodily function, or an organ. State restrictions on protected reproductive care, or on people helping someone obtain it, would have to be narrowly tailored to protect the patient’s health through the least restrictive means. Providers could not face professional discipline or civil or criminal liability solely for helping someone exercise these rights in a way consistent with the act. Existing malpractice rules and providers’ freedom-of-conscience protections would remain. The act would not require the state to pay for the protected care or limit existing rights or access to reproductive care. It would take effect January 1, 2027. Idaho’s fiscal office estimates $3,100 to $7,800 in additional annual state costs for Medicaid-covered treatment of complications from medication abortions.
measureRecords.yesMeans: A YES vote would adopt these reproductive health care rights and protections, including abortion before viability and in the defined medical emergencies after viability.
measureRecords.noMeans: A NO vote would reject this act and leave Idaho’s existing law unchanged by this measure.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: This nonbinding advisory question asks voters to choose one preferred official Idaho state gun from six options: Winchester Model 1894 (.30-30); Winchester Model 1873 “Gun that Won the West” (.44-40); 1873 Colt Single Action Army Revolver “Peacemaker” (.45 Colt); M1 Garand rifle (.30-06); Colt M1911 .45 automatic Colt pistol (.45 ACP); or Remington Model 700 bolt-action rifle (.30-06). It is a choice among those guns, rather than a YES-or-NO vote. The result would not designate a state gun by itself: the Legislature would have to act in a future session.
